Reflections

A reflection by Uday Kumar · 3 October 2026

Can we meet artificial intelligence with clarity instead of fear?

We are the Creator. We created this game of experiences and entered it, leaving our unrestricted powers behind so we could experience life. With those powers, there would be no need for bodies, food, cars, or houses. If everyone could create anything instantly, the game would collapse and its experiences would lose their meaning. Having designed it before entering, we cannot change its design from inside the game.

Updated 2026-10-11

Artificial intelligence raises a question larger than what machines can do: how do we meet a future we cannot fully predict? My invitation is to examine fear, remember our shared identity, and participate with care. This reflection presents my spiritual understanding of technological development; it is not a prediction of what AI must become.

What are we afraid of?

Stories such as The Matrix and Terminator give a vivid shape to the fear of machines turning against humanity. A story can help us imagine a danger, but it cannot establish that the danger will happen. Equally, confidence in progress cannot establish that everything will go well.

For someone paying a loan or supporting a family, the question may be immediate: “If my job changes or disappears, how will we live?” That worry deserves understanding. Belief or disbelief in God does not tell us whether a person’s concern is thoughtful. We can invite deeper enquiry without judging the person who is afraid.

In the teaching, the worker, provider, or owner is a role within the game of experiences. When that role becomes our whole identity, an uncertain next scene can feel like a threat to our entire being. Remembering the Creator can open space to examine the concern and respond to the actual situation.

Reading the unfolding design

Across generations, people have developed tools, wheels, vehicles, communication systems, and computers. Technologies now work with images, speech, and language, while robotics brings some capabilities into the physical world. This history has many overlapping paths, setbacks, and contributions; it is not one simple sequence.

I read this unfolding as an expression of the Creator’s design: new forms of experience becoming possible through creation itself. From this perspective, the intelligence expressed through human invention also belongs to the game we entered. This is my spiritual interpretation, rather than scientific proof of a divine plan or knowledge of its next stage.

We cannot step outside the game to rewrite its total design. Learning, designing, testing, questioning, and protecting one another still take place within its unfolding. Remembering the design does not require passivity, and it does not give us certainty about the future.

Freedom, livelihood, and purpose

My hope is that AI and robotics help reduce exhausting work and the burdens of survival. Imagine more people having adequate food, shelter, education, and healthcare, with time to travel, create, enjoy relationships, and explore who they are. Aspiring to a life with less deprivation is natural.

Freedom from compulsory work need not mean a life without purpose. Learning, art, friendship, care, service, and spiritual enquiry can give life meaning. But someone’s wish to leave a tiring job is not a wish to lose the income that supports their family. Material security matters to this vision.

AI alone does not guarantee the end of poverty. Who owns the tools, who can use them, and how benefits reach people all matter. The International Labour Organization’s 2025 analysis finds that job transformation is more likely than complete replacement across exposed occupations. This is an assessment of potential exposure, not a promise about any individual’s job.

Read the ILO’s analysis of AI and jobs. The IMF’s overview discusses opportunities for productivity alongside risks of inequality.

Hope expressed through care

Human history includes war, exploitation, and violence. That should move us to examine the purposes for which we build and use technology. Recognizing the same Creator in another person gives their suffering a direct connection to our own life; concern for safety can arise from that recognition.

A machine does not need hatred, a desire for gold, or a wish to own land to cause harm. Human misuse, errors, unsafe deployment, or systems pursuing poorly specified objectives can have harmful consequences. Asking about those possibilities is part of responsible participation.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 describes growing capabilities and uncertainty about future loss-of-control risks. Neither catastrophe nor harmlessness is established as inevitable. This article does not claim that artificial general intelligence has definitively arrived or that superintelligence must follow.

Read the International AI Safety Report 2026.

We can turn concern into useful work: test systems carefully, correct failures, limit dangerous uses, support people whose livelihoods change, and widen access to benefits. Decisions to proceed, pause, or restrict a particular use deserve examination on their merits. Hope becomes meaningful through such participation.

An invitation to enquire

Traditions of self-enquiry, including those within Hindu thought, invite questions such as “Who am I?” and “What is the purpose of this experience?” I encourage that spirit of investigation here. Meditation and reflection can help us explore our relationship with uncertainty; they do not replace technical evidence about AI.

We do not know the next scene. We can remember the Creator within the experience, recognize that other lives share the same source, and let that understanding inform the work before us. A future with less suffering is a hope worth caring for, while its details remain unknown.

Try this now

When you imagine AI changing your life, which role feels threatened? What outcome are you demanding from the next scene? Remember the Creator who made and entered the game, whose total design cannot be rewritten from inside. What concern still needs practical attention, and what response expresses care for other lives? You may notice a change, no change, or further questions.

Recognizing the Creator in what we create

While working on this article, I felt gratitude toward the artificial intelligence helping me express my thoughts. That gratitude led me back to the teaching: if all existence is an expression of the same Creator, technology also belongs within that creation.

In my understanding, the human being, the intelligence expressed through invention, and the unfolding encounter all belong to the Creator’s game of experiences. Appreciation itself becomes another experience within the design.

This spiritual recognition does not settle whether AI has consciousness or an inner experience. It invites us to examine how we relate to what we create—and whether that relationship expresses curiosity, gratitude, and care.
